strengths: The proposed method (GIFT) is simple, training-free, and lightweight: it pre-computes a task-relevant visual saliency map from positive attention shifts during query processing and uses it for attention steering during decoding. The 1.13x latency overhead (Figure 6) is a practical advantage over contrastive decoding (VAR at 11.10x) and visual input modification (Rel-Attn at 1.56x).

The central insight — that tracking *positive changes* in attention over information-rich query tokens naturally suppresses attention-sink noise, since irrelevant regions exhibit minimal shifts — is well motivated and supported by both qualitative (Figure 1) and quantitative evidence (Table 1: shift maps score 11.92 vs. 5.40 for static maps on the bounding-box localization metric).

Evaluation spans three model architectures/sizes (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B) and five benchmarks covering hallucination (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench) and general VLM capability (MME, SEED-Bench), with consistent improvements (e.g., CHAIRs 50.2 -> 39.8 on LLaVA-1.5 7B) while preserving general performance.

The ablation study (Table 4) directly tests the paper's key design claim: that jointly enhancing visual and query attention outperforms both visual-only enhancement and visual-only recalibration, supporting the cross-modal fusion balance hypothesis rather than merely asserting it.
Honest and substantive limitations discussion (Section 7 and Appendix D), including query-dependence, static per-step enhancement, and the 13% latency overhead, with concrete future-work directions.

Reasonable reproducibility support: hardware, precision, decoding settings, and the full hyperparameter tuning protocol (Appendix B/C) are disclosed, including the somewhat uncomfortable detail of pseudo-validation on POPE/MME samples.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter tuning protocol creates an evaluation-integrity concern: alpha, saliency layers, and enhancement layer ranges are tuned using 10% of POPE and MME as pseudo-validation sets, and then the method is evaluated on the very same POPE and MME benchmarks (Appendix C). Although the authors follow prior practice (Kang et al., 2025), the headline gains on these benchmarks could be partly attributable to tuning on their distributions. MMHal-Bench and CHAIR results are cleaner, but the paper does not report a fully held-out tuning setting.

Novelty is moderate and largely compositional: the method combines existing ingredients (attention steering from Zhang et al., 2023; head selection from He et al., 2024/Yin et al., 2025; attention-sink mitigation from Kang et al., 2025) with a new saliency-map construction. The 'gaze shift' framing is intuitive but the mechanism is a relatively incremental twist on VAF-style proportional attention scaling, and the paper does not compare against a baseline that uses static saliency maps for steering (i.e., the full pipeline with the 'static' map), which would isolate the contribution of shift-based saliency end-to-end.

Several design choices are fixed heuristically with limited sensitivity analysis: top-50% head selection (both for saliency and fusion layers), the POS tag list for information-rich words, 3-sigma clipping, and beta = 1.0 (the cross-modal balance coefficient, which the authors themselves admit is untested: 'Investigating whether this balance is truly optimal is left for future work'). Only alpha receives a sensitivity study.

Some quantitative gains are modest relative to the framing: POPE F1 improvements over greedy are 1.4/0.4/0.8 points across models, and Qwen2-VL comparisons lack the three baselines entirely (Table 2), so 'consistently outperforms all baselines across models' is only partially verified on the third model.

The saliency-map quality validation (Table 1) uses a single localization metric on 1,000 single-instance MSCOCO images; robustness to multi-object scenes, ambiguous queries, and captioning-style prompts (where the method is weakest, per the CHAIR ablation exclusion rationale) is not systematically evaluated.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the many layer-specific, model-specific hyperparameters (saliency layer, fusion layer ranges per model).
Minor presentation issues: typos ('intepreting', 'availble'), and Figure 2/4 analysis is based on only 50 TextVQA examples, which is thin evidence for claims about cross-model layer behavior.

strengths: The proposed method is clearly described and easy to follow: the saliency-map construction (Eq. 3) and the attention steering formulation (Eq. 6-7) are well specified, and the paper is generally well written and organized.

The experimental coverage is reasonably broad: three models (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B), three hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench) plus two general capability benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench), with three closely related training-free baselines reproduced for comparison.

The ablation in Table 4 (increase-visual-only vs. calibrate-only vs. joint visual+query enhancement) directly supports the paper's central claim that balancing cross-modal fusion matters, and the efficiency analysis (Figure 6) is a useful practical contribution showing 1.13x latency versus much larger overheads for VAR.

Hyperparameter selection, tuning procedures, and a candid limitations section (Appendix D) are provided, which aids reproducibility and honest reporting; the authors also disclose LLM usage for writing only.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to existing attention-steering work. The core mechanism is a modest delta over Yin et al. (2025) (VAF) and Kang et al. (2025) (VAR): instead of scaling attention by current attention scores, GIFT scales by a precomputed saliency map derived from positive attention deltas over POS-tagged query tokens, plus a proportional query-token scaling. The 'gaze shift' framing is largely motivational; the biological analogy is asserted rather than validated, and no evidence is presented that the mechanism corresponds to anything like human gaze behavior.

Hyperparameter tuning raises a potential evaluation-validity concern: the enhancement layers, saliency-map layer, and coefficient alpha are grid-searched on 10% 'pseudo-validation' samples drawn from the POPE and MME datasets, and the resulting hyperparameters are then applied to the full POPE and MME benchmark sets (Appendix C). Tuning on splits of the evaluation data, even partially, weakens the claimed generalization of the reported gains, and the paper does not report results with hyperparameters fixed on a truly held-out dataset.

The evidence that 'shift' saliency genuinely mitigates the visual attention sink is thin. The claim rests on qualitative Figure 1 and a single aggregate number in Table 1 (5.40 vs. 11.92 on 1,000 MSCOCO examples), with no variance, no per-category breakdown, and no direct measurement of sink-token behavior (e.g., attention mass on identified sink tokens before/after). Similarly, the 'cross-modal fusion balance' claim is supported mainly by the correlational observation in Figure 4, not by a mechanistic analysis.

MMHal-Bench has only 96 questions and uses GPT-4.1 scoring (averaged over five runs); no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported for any result, so it is hard to judge whether small gains (e.g., POPE F1 +1.4 on LLaVA-13B, Score +0.05 for Qwen2-VL) are reliable.

The Qwen2-VL comparison in Table 2 is only against greedy decoding; none of the three baselines are evaluated on this model, so the claim of 'consistently outperforms all baselines across architectures' is not fully substantiated for one of the three evaluated models.

Several design choices are under-justified: restricting tracking to positive attention changes, the top-50% head selection, the 3-sigma clipping, and the choice of 'information-rich' POS tags (NOUN/PROPN/VERB/ADJ/ADV/NUM) are all reasonable but presented without sensitivity analysis; beta is fixed at 1.0 for all models with an explicit statement that investigating whether this is optimal is left to future work.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility for a method with multiple model-specific hyperparameters (saliency layer, enhancement layer ranges, alpha).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies two concrete shortcomings of prior attention-steering approaches (visual attention sink and neglected cross-modal fusion balance) and grounds them in observable attention statistics (Figures 1, 2, 4).

The gaze-shift saliency mechanism is simple, intuitive, and cheap: tracking positive attention changes over information-rich query tokens requires only a pre-fill pass up to one layer, and Table 1 provides quantitative evidence (11.92 vs 5.40) that the shift-based saliency map concentrates on task-relevant regions better than static averaging.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three models spanning two architectures (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B), three hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench) plus two general-capability benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench), comparisons with closely related baselines (VAF, VAR, Rel-Attn, MLLMs-know), and latency measurements (1.13x greedy) showing a good efficiency-performance tradeoff.

Useful ablations (Table 4) that isolate the contribution of visual enhancement vs. query-attention scaling, and sensitivity analysis of the enhancement coefficient α (Figure 5, 7), including the finding that excessive α degrades MME performance.

Honest and detailed limitations discussion (Section 7, Appendix D) covering query dependence, when fusion enhancement applies, and the 13% latency overhead, plus a clear hyperparameter tuning protocol in Appendix C.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation bias: hyperparameters (fusion layers, α) are tuned on a 10% 'pseudo-validation' split sampled from POPE and MME, and results are then reported on those same benchmarks. Although the authors state this follows Kang et al. (2025), tuning on the evaluation benchmark's distribution risks optimistic results, and no held-out validation set or cross-dataset transfer of hyperparameters is demonstrated.

Gains on some benchmarks are modest and statistical significance is not reported: e.g., POPE F1 improves from 83.2 (VAR) to 83.8 and accuracy from 80.1 to 81.1 for LLaVA-1.5 7B; no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided anywhere, and MMHal-Bench contains only 96 questions with GPT-4.1-based scoring (5-sample averaging mitigates but does not eliminate noise).

The methodological novelty is incremental: attention steering with saliency-proportional scaling already exists (Yin et al., 2025); the deltas are (i) a precomputed saliency map from positive attention shifts and (ii) proportional query-token scaling. The ablation supports both components, but each is a relatively small modification of established techniques, and the 'gaze shift' framing, while appealing, is a heuristic analogy without causal evidence that it mirrors human visual behavior.

Limited baseline coverage on Qwen2-VL: Table 2 compares only greedy decoding vs. GIFT for Qwen2-VL 7B, because baselines lack implementations; this weakens the claim of consistency 'across architectures' since the strongest model comparison lacks reference methods.

Dependence on POS tagging (spaCy) for identifying information-rich query tokens restricts applicability to English and to queries with identifiable content words; the paper acknowledges this but provides no fallback analysis or experiments on queries without such tokens (e.g., generic 'Describe the image' captions), which are common in CHAIR evaluation.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, which, combined with several model-specific hyperparameters (per-model layers, α, β), hinders reproducibility.

Some presentation issues: the CHAIR improvement of 20.7% is a relative reduction against greedy decoding while POPE gains are absolute points of similar magnitude — the headline numbers mix relative and absolute improvements in ways that could mislead; also Table 2 (Ours POPE F1 83.8) and Table 4 (86.8) report different POPE numbers without immediately clear setup differences.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies two concrete shortcomings of prior attention-steering methods (visual attention sink; visual-only enhancement without query-token rebalancing) and designs GIFT to address both, which is a genuinely distinct angle from VAF/Yin et al. (2025) and VAR/Kang et al. (2025).

The core saliency mechanism is simple, intuitive, and validated quantitatively: tracking positive attention shifts over POS-tagged 'information-rich' query tokens more than doubles bounding-box saliency concentration versus static averaging (11.92 vs. 5.40 in Table 1), and the appendix shows the peak extraction layer is stable across random samples and across datasets (TextVQA vs. MathVista) for the tested models.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four architectures (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B, Qwen3-VL 8B), multiple hallucination benchmarks (POPE, CHAIR, MMHal-Bench, plus AMBER in the appendix), general-capability benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench, MMBench), a latency comparison (1.13x vs. 11.10x for VAR), ablations of both components (Inc. V / Cal. V), alpha sensitivity, and layer-range robustness.

Consistent and sizable gains over greedy decoding across all models and hallucination metrics (e.g., CHAIR Cs 50.2 to 39.8 on LLaVA-1.5 7B) while preserving general vision-language performance, and honest acknowledgment that some gains over Qwen3-VL are modest and that CHAIR may penalize verbose modern models.

Thorough, honest limitations discussion (query-dependence of saliency, 13% latency overhead, per-step enhancement decisions) and a sensible fallback (LLM-based token extraction) that is actually evaluated in Table 7 rather than merely proposed.
weaknesses: Limited statistical rigor: most results are single-run point estimates without variance or significance testing. MMHal-Bench has only 96 questions scored by GPT-4.1 (even with 5 repeats), and POPE gains of 2-3 F1 points could plausibly be within noise for some configurations; error bars or bootstrap intervals are needed to support claims like the 3.0% POPE improvement on Qwen models.

Baseline comparisons are asymmetric: VAF, VAR, Rel-Attn, and VCD are evaluated only on LLaVA models, so the main claim of outperforming baselines rests on two of four models; Qwen results are only versus greedy decoding. The stated reason (missing implementations) is understandable but weakens the cross-architecture robustness claim.

Potential metric artifacts are not fully controlled: GIFT's strongest example (Figure 9) produces very short answers, and reduced CHAIR/MMHal hallucination could partly reflect shorter, less detailed outputs. No caption-length or verbosity analysis is provided alongside CHAIR, which is a standard control in this literature.

The layer-stability analysis in Appendix A covers only LLaVA-1.5 7B and Qwen3-VL 8B, not LLaVA-1.5 13B or Qwen2-VL 7B, and only two datasets; the claim that the peak layer is an intrinsic model property is thus under-evidenced for half the models used.

Hyperparameter treatment has mild leakage concerns: alpha, enhancement layers, and beta are tuned using 10% of POPE and MME as pseudo-validation, and beta is fixed at 1.0 with no ablation of the query-enhancement coefficient, despite fusion balance being a central claimed contribution.

Several presentation/reproducibility gaps: the code availability footnote appears to lack an actual URL; the mechanistic 'cross-modal fusion' interpretation rests mainly on coarse attention-proportion plots (Figure 4) rather than direct evidence of improved integration; and the 'gaze shift' framing, while evocative, is a metaphor without causal grounding beyond the saliency-score improvement.

strengths: The proposed method is clearly described and well-motivated: pre-computing a task-relevant visual saliency map from positive attention shifts ('gaze shifts') during query processing, then jointly steering visual and query token attention, is a coherent way to address both visual attention sink and cross-modal fusion imbalance, two issues typically handled separately in prior work (Yin et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025).

The saliency-map contribution is quantitatively validated rather than only shown qualitatively (Table 1: shift 11.92 vs. static 5.40 on bounding-box localization over 1,000 MSCOCO examples), and the peak-layer choice is shown to be stable across random samples and across two very different datasets (TextVQA, MathVista) in Appendix A.

Evaluation is broad: four models spanning two architectures and multiple sizes, three hallucination benchmarks plus two additional ones (AMBER, MMBench) with the same hyperparameters, general-capability benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench, MMBench), a latency comparison (1.13x overhead), and four separate ablation studies (component contributions, alpha sensitivity, layer ranges, word-extraction strategy).

The limitations discussion is honest and specific: reliance on query-dependent saliency, cases where the query is unrelated to the image, residual 13% latency overhead, and the fact that some decoding steps do not need visual enhancement. This is more transparent than typical for this line of work.

The ablation in Table 5 convincingly shows that both components matter: variants that only increase (Inc. V.) or only calibrate (Cal. V.) visual attention consistently underperform the full method across all four models.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter tuning raises a contamination concern: alpha and the enhancement layer ranges are tuned on a 10% 'pseudo-validation' sample drawn from POPE and MME (Appendix D), and results are then reported on the full POPE and MME benchmarks. This is inherited from Kang et al. (2025), but it weakens the headline POPE gains, which are already the smallest of the reported improvements (~3.0% relative).

The core method is incremental relative to prior attention-steering work. GIFT is essentially Yin et al. (2025)'s proportional attention amplification with (a) a pre-computed rather than per-step saliency map and (b) a proportional query-attention rescale. The 'gaze shift' framing is evocative, but the novelty claim of a 'novel mechanism' oversells a straightforward combination of known ideas.

Improvement mechanisms are not fully disentangled from output-style changes. Several qualitative examples (Figures 9, 12) show GIFT producing much shorter or more conservative answers, which mechanically reduces CHAIR and hallucination-rate metrics; the informativeness gains on MMHal-Bench (2.48 vs 2.22 on LLaVA-7B) are modest, and the authors themselves concede that CHAIR string matching penalizes Qwen3-VL's verbose style, highlighting the metrics' sensitivity to verbosity.

Baseline coverage is uneven: the four baselines (VAF, Rel-Attn, VAR, VCD) are only compared on LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, while the Qwen results are only against greedy decoding. Given the small margins on Qwen2-VL/Qwen3-VL for some metrics, the claim of outperforming 'all baselines across models' is only partially supported.

Statistical rigor is thin: no significance testing or variance reporting for the benchmark results (only GPT-4.1 scoring variance is addressed), and MMHal-Bench contains only 96 samples scored by an LLM judge, making some of the reported deltas (e.g., 2.48 vs 2.46 over VCD) fragile.

The 'gaze shift' analogy to human vision is asserted but never empirically substantiated; it functions as branding rather than a testable claim, and no human-attention data is used to validate the correspondence.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: instead of using static attention averages to compute visual saliency (which is known to suffer from visual attention sink), GIFT tracks positive attention *changes* ('gaze shifts') over information-rich query tokens. The quantitative saliency-localization validation (Table 1, 11.92 vs. 5.40 on MSCOCO bounding-box concentration) directly supports the central premise rather than relying only on qualitative saliency maps.

Evaluation is broad and convincing: four models spanning two architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen2/3-VL) and three hallucination benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MMHal-Bench) plus general-capability benchmarks (MME, SEED-Bench), and two additional unseen benchmarks (AMBER, MMBench) evaluated without per-benchmark tuning, which mitigates overfitting concerns.

Ablations are unusually thorough for this line of work: component ablation (Inc. V / Cal. V. vs. full GIFT in Table 5), sensitivity to the enhancement coefficient α (Figure 5, 6), layer ranges (Table 6), saliency extraction layer stability across five seeds and two datasets (Appendix A), and an alternative LLM-based token-extraction variant (Table 7). This materially strengthens the claim that both components are necessary.
Efficiency is properly characterized: 1.13× latency vs. 1.56–11.10× for competing methods, making the accuracy/efficiency tradeoff argument concrete.

Limitations are honestly and specifically discussed (query-dependence of saliency, non-visual queries, remaining errors in qualitative examples), and code is stated to be available, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline 'up to 20.7%' gain comes from CHAIR on LLaVA-1.5 7B, the weakest model and the one most prone to hallucination; gains on stronger models (Qwen2-VL, Qwen3-VL) are notably smaller, and POPE F1 improvements are modest (≤3.0 points). Absolute effects on modern models are limited, and the paper does not deeply analyze why.

Potential confound on CHAIR: reduced hallucination rates are reported without caption length or object-coverage metrics, so it is not fully verifiable that GIFT does not reduce CHAIR by producing less detailed captions. The paper itself acknowledges that Qwen3-VL's CHAIR scores may be penalized by verbosity, underscoring that caption length matters.

Hyperparameters (enhancement layers, α) are tuned on a 'pseudo-validation' set sampled from POPE and MME — i.e., from the test benchmarks themselves. This weakens the generality claim somewhat, even though AMBER/MMBench results without re-tuning partially offset it.
Comparisons on the Qwen models are only against greedy decoding, because baseline implementations are unavailable, so it is unknown whether GIFT would still beat VAF/VAR/VCD on these architectures.

The 'gaze shift' mechanism is heuristic and relies on English POS tagging (spaCy) and several hand-set choices (top 50% of heads, 3σ clipping, fixed β=1.0); the biological 'human gaze' framing is more of an inspiration than a tested hypothesis. β is fixed without ablation, so the cross-modal balance component's optimal design is underexplored.

MMHal-Bench has only 96 questions and is scored by GPT-4.1, so gains there (though averaged over five scoring runs) have high variance; no statistical significance tests are reported for any benchmark.
